newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. envoy to meet Zaire rebel leader.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy to meet Zaire rebel leader.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun flew to the northeastern Zairean city of Kisangani on Saturday for talks with Zaire's rebel leader Laurent Kabila, diplomats said.
They said Sahnoun, joint envoy of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, was believed to be carrying a special message and proposals for a ceasefire in Zaire.
"He has gone to see Kabila. We are made to understand that he is carrying a special message for Kabila," a diplomat told Reuters.
"We are also made to understand he is going to present new proposals on a possibility for a ceasefire in Zaire," said the diplomat, who asked not to be identified.

A political source told Reuters that Kabila was coming under heavy pressure to call a ceasefire, especially after President Mobutu Sese Seko said on Thursday he no longer ruled out talks with the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).
"He is under immense pressure to call for a ceasefire and he now risks being labelled 'the bad boy' if he continues to refuse to do so," the source said.
Sahnoun was expected to head for the capital Kinshasa, where Mobutu arrived on Friday, after talks with Kabila, diplomats said.
Sahnoun on Friday discussed the crisis with Ugandan president and regional power broker Yoweri Museveni in the northern Ugandan town of Gulu before returning to Nairobi overnight.
Museveni, a close ally of Kabila, also met European Union envoy Aldo Ajello. On Thursday last week, Sahnoun visited Museveni and Kabila in Gulu and the rebel leader rejected a plea for a ceasefire.
On Friday, Kabila arrived in the northeast Zairean capital of Kisangani and reiterated his position of demanding negotiations with Mobutu, or a representative appointed by him, before any ceasefire.
The international community is banking on Museveni's influence in the region to push Kabila into a ceasefire. The rebels have seized more than one-fifth of Zaire since October.

Kabila received a hero's welcome on Friday on his first visit to Kisangani since the rebels captured the city a week ago. He has said he will only negotiate over the terms for the ailing Zairean leader to step down.
Mobutu, who left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after cancer treatment, called on Thursday for a truce and a Zairean national council to find a peace settlement.
Mobutu's son, Nzanga, said in France on Thursday that his father no longer ruled out talks with the rebels but wanted to involve the government, army and transitional parliament.

Mobutu, 66, has spent almost all his time in Europe since prostate cancer surgery in August. He has dominated Zaire with a mixture of political acumen and military ruthlessness since seizing power in 1965.

Kabila's rebel force is dominated by ethnic Tutsis, some of them Zairean Banyamulenge Tutsis and others said by intelligence sources to be members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army. The Rwandan government denies any involvement with the rebels.
Demobilised Ugandan troops, hired on contract, are also part of the rebel force. Kabila is a Zairean non-Tutsi from Shaba and his field commanders are a mixture of Zaireans and foreigners.
